newsitem.title: USA: U.S. fixed-rate mortgages fall to 4-month lows.
newsitem.headline: U.S. fixed-rate mortgages fall to 4-month lows.

text.p: Mortgage rates fell this week for the fourth consecutive week to the lowest level in more than four months for fixed-rate loans, Freddie Mac said Thursday.
Thirty-year mortgages averaged 7.58 percent in the week ending June 27, below 7.61 percent last week. The rate has not been lower since it stood at 7.56 percent in the week ended Feb. 21, 1997.
Fifteen-year mortgages inched down to 7.13 percent from 7.14 percent, a level also not seen since the Feb. 21 week, when rates averaged 7.06 percent.
One-year adjustable mortgage rates were unchanged at 5.66 percent in the week. The rate has not been lower since it stood at 5.61 percent in the week ended March 14, Freddie Mac said.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 8.29 percent, the 15-year 7.82 percent and the adjustable loan 5.98 percent.

"The market continues to feel that inflation is no threat at the present time and that the Federal Reserve will take little, if any, action when it meets in July," Robert Van Order, Freddie Mac chief economist, said in a statement.
"Thus, interest rates remain affordably low right now, though they may inch back up a bit next week."
Lenders charged an average of 1.7 percent in fees and points on 30- and 15-year loans, and 1.5 percent on adjustable loans, all unchanged from last week.
Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
